title: What You Flush Can End Up on a Farm Field #shorts
summary: Sewage solids settle out, spend about 15 days in digesters heated to about 98°F where microbes make biogas (NYC DEP), and what's left is treated into biosolids. In 2024, 59.5% of the sludge reported to EPA was land applied.
sources: Biosolids are sewage sludge treated to meet EPA Part 503 standards, intended for land application on agricultural land, forests, rangelands and other sites; in 2024 about 4 million dry metric tons of sewage sludge was reported, of which 59.5 percent was land applied and 14 percent incinerated (2024 Biosolids Annual Reports, about 2,350 reporting facilities only) (US EPA, Basic Information about Sewage Sludge and Biosolids): https://www.epa.gov/biosolids/basic-information-about-sewage-sludge-and-biosolids

NYC treatment: bar screens; primary settling tanks where the flow slows down and heavier sludge settles; air added so oxygen-loving microorganisms consume much of the organic material; final settling; disinfection with sodium hypochlorite, the same chemical found in household bleach; after about 8-10 hours the facilities release clean water; digesters heated to about 98°F for about 15 days, where microorganisms convert much of the material into biogas, which can produce heat and electricity for the facilities (NYC DEP, Wastewater Treatment System): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/wastewater-treatment-process.page

scenes.narration: What you flush can end up on a farm.
At the plant, solids sit in digesters at about {98°F|ninety-eight degrees} for about {15|fifteen} days.
Microbes turn much of it into biogas, for heat and power.
What's left is treated into biosolids. In {2024|twenty twenty-four}, {59.5%|fifty-nine and a half percent} of reported sludge went onto land.
